groups.name: Cells named after people
groups.explanation: Each clue points to a cell that carries someone's name.

article.text: All four are cells with a person's name attached, and each one points to a specific disease or organ.

CD15+ and CD30+: the immunostain profile of the Reed-Sternberg cell (named for Dorothy Reed and Carl Sternberg). It is the large binucleate owl-eye cell of classical Hodgkin lymphoma; the nodular lymphocyte-predominant type lacks classic Reed-Sternberg cells.

Heart slide: Anitschkow cells (Nikolai Anitschkow), activated macrophages whose chromatin bunches into a wavy bar, the caterpillar nucleus. They sit inside Aschoff bodies, the granulomas of rheumatic myocarditis after group A strep pharyngitis.
Liver slide, iron stain: a Kupffer cell (Karl von Kupffer), the resident macrophage lining the hepatic sinusoids. It has eaten iron, which the Prussian blue stain shows as blue granules.

Langhans giant cell (Theodor Langhans): macrophages fused into one large cell with nuclei arranged in a horseshoe at the edge. It is typical of granulomas, especially caseating granulomas in tuberculosis. Not to be confused with Langerhans cells of the skin.

Images: Wikimedia Commons, "Anitschkow Myocytes in an Aschoff Body, Rheumatic Myocarditis", Ed Uthman, MD, CC BY-SA 2.0; Wikimedia Commons, "Kupffer cell with hemosiderin and hepatocyte with lipofuscin, iron stain, original", Mikael Häggström, MD, CC0

items.label: Sepsis
items.note: Sepsis is a frequent etiology of distributive shock

items.label: Tension pneumothorax
items.note: One of the complications of a tension pneumothorax is obstructive shock

items.label: Papillary muscle rupture
items.note: Papillary muscle rupture can lead to acute mitral regurgitation and cardiogenic shock

items.label: Penetrating trauma
items.note: Penetrating trauma is a common cause of hypovolemic/hemorrhagic shock

items.label: Low ceruloplasmin
items.note: Usually evident in late childhood or early adolescence, these rings develop due to excess copper deposition on the inner surface of the cornea within the Descemet membrane

items.label: Zinc acetate
items.note: Zinc (such as zinc acetate or Galzin) blocks the intestines from absorbing copper from your food. It is commonly used for maintenance treatment after initial copper levels have been safely lowered, or for asymptomatic patients.

items.label: Signet Rings in gastric adenocarcinoma
items.note: "signet rings" on H&E stain is the hallmark sign of an aggressive diffuse-type of adenocarcinoma of the stomach, the ring appearance due to the mucin pushing the nucleus to the periphery

items.label: Kayser-Fleischer Rings
items.note: Kayser-Fleischer rings are characteristic of Wilson's disease and are due to deposits of copper within Descemet's membrane

items.label: Signet rings in bronchiectasis
items.note: Signet rings on CT scan can be a classic sign of bronchiectasis

items.label: Ring-enhancing lesions on CT
items.note: Cerebral toxoplasmosis is the most common cause of intracranial ring-enhancing lesions in immunocompromised patients

items.label: CD15+ and CD30+
items.note: Reed-Sternberg cell, the owl-eye cell of Hodgkin lymphoma.

items.label: Heart, H&E
items.note: Anitschkow cell: the caterpillar nucleus, inside Aschoff bodies of rheumatic myocarditis.

items.label: Liver, iron stain
items.note: Kupffer cell, the resident macrophage of the liver sinusoids. Iron stain turns the hemosiderin it has eaten blue.

items.label: Langhans giant cell
items.note: Named for Theodor Langhans. Horseshoe of nuclei, found in granulomas such as TB.
